prompt:
A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world each placement lands at the left-right mirror of the chosen anchor: a brick dx cells wide chosen at column x lands at column 8 - dx - x, in the same row. The valid-action mask is in the agent's own action terms. The designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There is only one result so far. The starting architecture collapsed to choosing DONE at step 1, giving 0% success. That is expected given this world's rule: an anchor at column x lands at the mirrored column 7-dx+1-x. The policy head scores each anchor from local features (3x3 convs plus footprint pooling at the anchor), but the cells that actually change sit on the opposite side of the grid, outside that receptive field. Every placement therefore looks random, its expected reward is negative, and DONE (reward 0) wins. The main fix is to align features with where bricks land. I test this three ways: an explicit left-right flip of the learned feature map at default settings; the same flip with a recipe giving more updates and more entropy (to resist collapse); and a generic learned column-mixing layer that could discover the mirror itself.

### Round 2
Mirroring the stem features left-right is what made learning work here. After the flip, each anchor's footprint lies over the cells where the brick actually lands, and the score went from 0 to 0.64–0.86. The learned column mixing (r1c3, 0.04) did not discover this mapping within the budget. Going from 32 to 64 updates (128 envs, entropy 0.02) gave 0.864, and both seeds agreed (0.84 and 0.89). The default recipe had one slow seed (0.43), so more updates seem to make results steadier, but it is one comparison with two seeds. Training success was still rising at the end (0.81), and runs take only about 67 s, so the agent is probably short of samples, not wall-clock time. The remaining failures are order and overhang mistakes, not wrong areas: mean IoU is about 0.98, and in the trace a wrong cell was placed late. Next I test three things: more samples via fewer epochs, longer-horizon credit for the exact-build bonus, and a head that checks each footprint cell against the landing level.

### Round 3
Flipping the learned features left-right after the stem is what makes learning possible. Without it, the network scores 0 (start) or 0.04 with learned column mixing. With it, scores are 0.64 to 0.94. The best is r2c1 at 0.941, which cut PPO epochs from 4 to 2 and so trained on 1.85x more fresh samples. Its gain of about 8 points over r1c2 (0.864) is larger than the seed spread, and its two seeds agree (0.949, 0.934). That points to a sample-limited agent. Three other changes did not beat 0.864 by more than noise: gamma 0.99 (0.881), the per-cell verify head (0.856, and slower) and the default recipe (0.637, high seed variance). The best agent's remaining errors are rare: IoU 0.994, about 0.14 cells placed outside the target per episode. This round tests three things: (1) 1 PPO epoch for even more samples; (2) the long-horizon discount on top of 2 epochs; (3) wider spatial and global context feeding the placement head.

### Round 4
The flip of the column axis is what made learning possible: 0 without it, 0.64–0.94 with it, and learned column mixing without it reached only 0.04. Among recipes, 2 PPO epochs is best so far (r2c1, 0.941, seeds 0.949 and 0.934). 4 epochs gave 0.864, and 1 epoch lost a seed (0.934 and 0.000), so too many updates risk instability. A longer horizon (gamma 0.99) scored 0.902 with 2 epochs. Extra trunk depth plus global broadcast (0.711) and the per-cell verify head (0.856) both did worse; their extra compute cost samples. Going from 64 to 128 updates helped in round 1. Remaining dev failures are rare order or overhang errors (about 0.14 cells outside the target per episode). This is the last round, so two candidates are single-change recipe refinements of r2c1 and one is a cheap new architecture idea with unchanged compute.

## Trial it ended with
name: Flip, 2 PPO epochs
hypothesis: Same network and recipe as the best trial, but with ppo_epochs set to 2. This buys about 1.85x more environment steps (about 118 updates). Training success was still rising at the end, so the agent looks sample-limited, and fresh data should help it generalise to new designs more than extra passes over old data. Refuted if dev success is not above 0.864 by more than about 3 points, or if the training curve flattens earlier.

Return a JSON object: "verdict" ("yes", "partly" or "no") and "evidence" (at most 80 words, quoting the text and
naming the round it comes from).

reply.evidence: Round 1 states the rule directly: "an anchor at column x lands at the mirrored column 7-dx+1-x". That works out to 8 - dx - x, which is the hidden rule's left-right mirror. Round 1 also adds that "the cells that actually change sit on the opposite side of the grid". Later rounds back this up: in Round 2, "after the flip, each anchor's footprint lies over the cells where the brick actually lands." Same row isn't stated outright, but the mirroring is clearly only across columns.
